tip: French can't say 'I think so' bare – it needs an object: je crois que oui is literally 'I believe that yes.' The 'que oui' is fixed.
Offrir looks like 'offer' but means to give as a gift: elle offre des fleurs = she gives flowers as a present, not merely offering them.
Faire la fête is 'to party' – literally 'to make the party.' French reaches for faire where English uses 'have': ils font la fête.
For food and drink, prendre (to take) means 'to have': tu prends un croissant = you're having a croissant, not grabbing one to go.
Mettre means 'to put,' so tu mets la table is literally 'you put the table' – French's way of saying 'you set the table.'
French doesn't say your back hurts – you 'have pain at' it: tu as mal au dos, literally 'you have evil at the back.' Pattern: avoir mal à + body part.
When an adjective comes before a plural noun, des shrinks to de: not des beaux rêves but de beaux rêves. Faites de beaux rêves!
Nous faisons is pronounced 'fuh-zon,' not 'fay-zon' – only in forms of faire does that ai go to a silent schwa. Nous faisons une promenade.
Du café means 'some coffee' – du (de + le) is the 'some' French won't drop even where English omits it: qui veut du café ?
Je suis désolé is literally 'I am devastated' – désoler means to distress or lay waste. French apologizes by claiming to be crushed.
No question word, no inversion – just lift your voice: tu es malade ? is a full question by intonation alone, marked only by the ?
